title: Slowed vs Nightcore: The Real Difference Explained
description: Slowed vs nightcore, explained: tempo, pitch, moods and when each edit fits your track. Compare the two styles, then make either one free in your browser.
heroText: One edit drags a song down to a dreamy crawl; the other pushes it into a bright, sped-up version. The difference comes down to two numbers: how fast the track plays and how high the pitch sits. Slowed edits drop both, which is why they sound like daycore or lo-fi music. Nightcore raises both. You can hear both in seconds with our free [slowed and reverb maker](/) and its [nightcore maker](/nightcore-maker/) route.

sections.title: The short answer
sections.body: Slowed and nightcore are opposite directions from the same starting point: the original recording. One drops the tempo and darkens it, the other lifts the tempo and brightens it.

items.body: Speed drops to roughly 0.75–0.85× of the original and pitch is nudged down a semitone or two, with 40–60% reverb. This tool's Classic preset is 0.80× speed, −2 semitones, 55% reverb and +4 dB bass. The mood is calm, hazy and late-night.
items.title: Slowed

items.body: Speed rises to about 1.25× and pitch climbs with it, with little or no reverb. This tool's Nightcore preset is 1.25× speed, +4 semitones, 12% reverb and no bass boost. The mood is bright, urgent and energetic.
items.title: Nightcore

items.body: Both styles move tempo away from 1× and both take the pitch with them, which is why a slowed track sounds deeper and a nightcore track sounds younger. On this tool they are two separate controls — the speed slider sets tempo, the pitch slider sets key in whole semitones — and the presets set both at once, in opposite directions.

items.body: Reverb smears each note into the space after it. At 55% on a slowed edit it turns a dry vocal into something that hangs in the air; at the nightcore preset's 12% it barely shows, because a fast track already feels packed. Rendering adds a tail of about 1.6 seconds whenever reverb is above zero.

sections.title: When to use each style
sections.body: Pick the style from the song and the platform you are posting to, not from habit.

items.body: R&B, indie ballads and trap with sung hooks take a tempo drop well. Slowing an already fast track can smear the lyrics. Add reverb and a little bass boost — the Classic preset's 55% and +4 dB — for the late-night sound.
items.title: Choose slowed when the song is slow already

items.body: Pop, dance and hyperpop survive a sped-up version best. The vocals rise but the rhythm tightens, which is the effect nightcore fans are after. The preset's +4 semitones are what make it read as nightcore rather than a record played fast.
items.title: Choose nightcore for fast, rhythmic tracks

items.body: Daycore keeps the slowed, lowered feel but stays gentle enough for full listens. Press the Daycore preset — 0.75× speed, −5 semitones, 40% reverb — for a slowed edit with restraint rather than maximum wash.
items.title: Daycore is the middle path

sections.title: Settings that translate well
sections.body: Small moves survive different speakers and platforms better than extreme ones. These are the values the presets apply, and the ranges you can push them to.

steps.body: Speed 0.80×, pitch −2 st, reverb 55%, bass +4 dB — press Classic Slowed + Reverb. Keep within 0.75–0.85× or lyrics start to smear; go to −4 st and 65% reverb only if the song is sparse.
steps.title: Slowed recipe

steps.body: Speed 1.25×, pitch +4 st, reverb 12%, bass 0 dB — press Nightcore. If the vocal sounds shrill, come back to 1.15× rather than adding effects to hide it.
steps.title: Nightcore recipe

steps.body: Drag the trim handles on the waveform, or type the start and end in seconds. Leave about 1.6 seconds at the end for the reverb tail, so the last note decays instead of getting clipped mid-word.

faq.question: Is slowed just nightcore in reverse?
faq.answer: Close. Both styles pull tempo away from the original and push pitch with it, in opposite directions. On this tool the Classic Slowed + Reverb preset is 0.80× speed, −2 semitones, 55% reverb and +4 dB bass; the Nightcore preset is 1.25× speed, +4 semitones, 12% reverb and no bass boost. The reverb and low end are the extra ingredients that make slowed its own sound rather than nightcore played backwards.

faq.question: What is daycore?
faq.answer: Daycore is the gentler slowed style: lower and softer than the classic edit, with less reverb, for full listens rather than short clips. The Daycore preset here is 0.75× speed, −5 semitones, 40% reverb and +4 dB bass — noticeably deeper than the 0.80× classic setting without turning the vocal to mud.

faq.question: Does nightcore damage audio quality?
faq.answer: Raising speed and pitch does not remove detail the way heavy compression does, but extreme settings make vocals thin and shrill. Staying at or below about 1.25× keeps the track listenable, and rendering WAV keeps the result at full 16-bit resolution; the MP3 export is 192 kbps, plenty for a social clip.

faq.question: Which style is better for TikTok?
faq.answer: Both work. Slowed + reverb suits emotional, late-night edits; sped-up versions suit dance and trend sounds. Load the file once, render a short trimmed version of each preset from the same original, and post whichever keeps the hook intact.

faq.question: Do I need to change pitch separately from speed?
faq.answer: On this tool, yes — speed and pitch are two independent controls. The speed slider changes tempo only, so a 0.80× track stays in its original key until you move the pitch slider. The presets do both at once: Classic slowed sets −2 semitones, Nightcore sets +4. If you move speed by hand, adjust pitch until the voice sounds natural.

faq.question: Can I convert between the two styles?
faq.answer: Yes. Load the same original file and press the other preset rather than editing an export, then render again. Every export should come from the original recording, because rendering an already-rendered MP3 changes the audio twice and loses detail each time.

faq.question: How are the settings in the table checked?
faq.answer: The table lists the settings each style normally uses — conventions shared by slowed and nightcore tools generally. The console on the maker pages shows the exact values this site's presets apply, so you can compare the convention with what you hear.
